[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Bumetanide, a structurally similar 5-sulfamoyl anthranilic acid loop diuretic, has absolute oral bioavailability of 95% in cirrhosis patients after 1 mg oral versus intravenous dosing.

Azosemide, the closest structural analog sharing the sulfamoyl anthranilate core, aryl chloride, and heteroarylmethylamino substituent, has absolute oral bioavailability of approximately 20.4% in fasted healthy humans, which meets the F >= 20% threshold.

In the same cirrhosis condition, metoclopramide shows absolute oral bioavailability of 79-82% and tolfenamic acid shows 91-100%, indicating that cirrhosis contexts in this evidence set consistently support F >= 20%.
No L1 record in any visible context reports an absolute oral bioavailability below 20%; the lowest relevant analog value is azosemide at 20.4%.

evidence_gaps: No direct oral bioavailability measurement exists for the query molecule itself.
Azosemide, the closest analog, was studied in fasted healthy subjects rather than cirrhosis patients.
The furan and chloro substituents of the query may alter first-pass metabolism relative to bumetanide and azosemide.
Cirrhosis effects on the query's specific transporter and metabolic pathways are not directly measured.
content.decision_summary: The empirical L1 record uniformly supports F >= 20%. The condition-matched cirrhosis contexts show high absolute bioavailability for structurally related acids (bumetanide 95%, tolfenamic acid 91-100%) and for metoclopramide (79-82%). The closest structural analog azosemide has F of 20.4%, which is at the threshold and therefore positive class. The physicochemical prior predicting low F is not affirmative threshold-relevant evidence and cannot override the consistent measured outcomes. Prediction is high with moderate confidence.

llm.reasoning_content:
The user wants me to perform a bioavailability_ma prediction for a query molecule under cirrhosis condition. Let me analyze the query molecule and the evidence.

Query molecule: NS(=O)(=O)c1cc(C(=O)O)c(NCc2ccco2)cc1Cl
This is a sulfonamide-substituted anthranilic acid derivative with a furan-containing benzylamine substituent and a chlorine. Let me parse: sulfonamide group (NS(=O)(=O)), carboxylic acid (C(=O)O), secondary amine (NCc2ccco2 where c2ccco2 is furan), and aryl chloride.

This looks like a loop diuretic analog - similar to azosemide (which has a tetrazole instead of carboxylic acid and a thiophene instead of furan) or bumetanide (which has a sulfamoyl group, carboxylic acid, phenoxy substituent, and butylamine). Actually the query is very similar to bumetanide: bumetanide is CCCC Nc1cc(C(=O)O)cc(S(N)(=O)=O)c1Oc1ccccc1 - 3-(butylamino)-4-phenoxy-5-sulfamoylbenzoic acid. The query has NCc2ccco2 (furfurylamino) instead of butylamino, and Cl instead of phenoxy. So it's a bumetanide/azosemide analog.

The external condition is cirrhosis. So the relevant contexts are those with disease=cirrhosis: bumetanide (F=95%), metoclopramide (F=79-82%), tolfenamic acid (F=91-100%). Also azosemide (fasted, F=20.4%) is structurally very similar to the query.

The query prior says low (F<20%) based on poor permeability (logD -2.53, fully ionized, high TPSA). But the instructions say the prior is uncertain and not endpoint proof. Predict low only when affirmative threshold-relevant evidence supports F<20%.

Let me look at the evidence contexts:

1. context_a73ee2a856dd05fd: PABA (4-aminobenzoic acid) in CF patients, F=90.1%. PABA is a small amino acid with carboxylic acid. Transfer likelihood 0.9939. This is a small molecule with carboxylic acid and amine. The query has a carboxylic acid and sulfonamide. PABA is much smaller and more permeable. Direction: high F, supportive of high. But transferability to query? PABA is small, zwitterionic, actively absorbed maybe. Hmm.

2. context_f8651334a40b426c: bumetanide in cirrhosis, F=95%. Bumetanide is structurally very similar to the query (both are 5-sulfamoyl-anthranilic acid derivatives with a substituent on the amine and an additional substituent). Bumetanide has butylamino and phenoxy; query has furfurylamino and chloro. Bumetanide F=95% in cirrhosis patients. This is highly transferable structurally and condition-matched (cirrhosis). Direction: supportive of high.

3. context_5dd124400838afdb: metoclopramide in cirrhosis, F=79-82%. Metoclopramide is a benzamide with diethylaminoethyl side chain. Condition-matched cirrhosis. Direction: high F, supportive of high. Transferability: moderate - different structure but same condition.

4. context_d1ba9f66a095028c: tolfenamic acid in cirrhosis, F=91-100%. Tolfenamic acid is a fenamate NSAID (anthranilic acid derivative with chloro and methylphenyl). Condition-matched cirrhosis. Structurally somewhat related (anthranilic acid). Direction: high.

5. context_fa99fc29ebcae441: amlodipine fasted, F=58%. Not condition-matched (fasted vs cirrhosis). Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine. Direction high but transferability low.

6. context_5a7554efc599d3c7: bromfenac fasted, F=67%. Bromfenac is an amino-phenylacetic acid with benzoyl. Fasting condition, not cirrhosis. Direction high.

7. context_4de516739663ddba: diclofenac fasted, F~50%. Anthranilic acid derivative (phenylacetic acid with dichlorophenyl amino). Fasting, not cirrhosis. Direction high (50% >= 20%).

8. context_c989497ce737a47d: azosemide fasted, F=20.4%. Azosemide is structurally very similar to the query: NS(=O)(=O)c1cc(-c2nn[nH]n2)c(NCc2cccs2)cc1Cl - it has sulfamoyl, tetrazole, thenylamino (thiophene-methyl-amino), and chloro. The query has sulfamoyl, carboxylic acid, furfurylamino, and chloro. Azosemide F=20.4% in healthy humans fasted. This is just above the 20% threshold. Direction: this is borderline - 20.4% is slightly above 20%, so it supports F>=20% barely, or is near-threshold. Actually for the F>=20% threshold, 20.4% is positive class (high). But it's very close to the threshold. The condition is fasted, not cirrhosis. Transferability: structurally very high (azosemide is nearly identical to query: same core, same sulfamoyl, same chloro, same secondary amine with heteroarylmethyl; only difference: tetrazole vs carboxylic acid, thiophene vs furan). 

9. context_e8176a6e3968c4a7: levodopa fasted, F=63.6-99%. Levodopa is an amino acid, actively transported. Fasting condition. Direction high.

10. context_697bbf08c41dc03d: PF-05241328, F=38%. No condition. PF-05241328 is a pyrazole-indole sulfonamide (a URAT1 inhibitor?). Direction high (38% >= 20%).

So all L1 evidence contexts show F values >= 20% (lowest is azosemide at 20.4%, which is just above threshold). None of the contexts show F < 20%.
